ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the collector node of transistor T is connected upward through collector resistor Rc to the +6 V power supply; the same collector node is also connected through output coupling capacitor C2 to the output terminal on the right side. Since C2 is a capacitor, for DC analysis it is equivalent to an open circuit. The left side of the base is connected to the input through input coupling capacitor C1, and is connected to the upper power supply through bias resistor Rb; the emitter is connected through Re to the bottom common terminal. Reasoning: The problem says that the emitter junction of the transistor is damaged and forms a short circuit. According to the method, regard it as a base-emitter junction short-circuit fault; the transistor cannot amplify normally, and the collector current is approximately Ic≈0. Since the collector current is approximately zero, there is no DC voltage drop across Rc. Therefore the potential of the collector node is pulled by Rc to the power-supply voltage, namely Uc=+6 V.

raw_record.question_text: In the circuit shown in figure 2, if the emitter junction of the transistor is damaged and forms a short circuit, what should the collector voltage \(U_c\) be?

method.method_draft: First describe the image: the collector of transistor T is connected upward through Rc to the +6 V supply, while the output coupling capacitor C2 is connected from the collector node and is open for DC. The text says the transistor's emitter junction is damaged and short-circuited. Treat this as a base-emitter junction short fault: the transistor cannot operate normally and is effectively cut off for collector current. Therefore Ic≈0, so Rc has no DC voltage drop. The collector node must rise to the supply rail, giving Uc = +6 V.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: Uc is the DC voltage at the transistor collector, below Rc; Rc is tied to the +6 V supply, and the output side is capacitor-coupled through C2. From the text, the emitter junction is shorted, so the base-emitter fault prevents a normal collector-emitter conduction path; the collector node has no DC current path to ground except through the nonconducting faulty transistor. Since C2 is open for DC, the only effective DC connection of the collector node is through Rc to +6 V. With no current through Rc, its voltage drop is 0, so the collector voltage equals the supply: Uc = 6 V.
